steps.body:
One function, differentiated twice, answers three different questions.

**s(t)** — where the particle IS.
**v(t) = s′(t)** — how fast, and which way.
**a(t) = v′(t) = s″(t)** — whether that is changing.

The sign of v is direction. The sign of a is not — and confusing the two is the classic error.

explanationVariants: s = t³ − 6t² + 9t gives v = 3t² − 12t + 9 and a = 6t − 12. At t = 1: a(1) = −6.
Each derivative is a fresh function — differentiate all the way down before substituting.

widget.prompt: s(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t. Find the acceleration at t = 1.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the VELOCITY at t = 1: v(1) = 3 − 12 + 9 = 0. The particle is momentarily at rest, but it is still accelerating: a(1) = 6 − 12 = −6.
That is the POSITION s(1) = 1 − 6 + 9 = 4. The acceleration is s″(1) = −6.
That is the coefficient in a = 6t − 12. Substitute t = 1: 6 − 12 = −6.

steps.body: Watch velocity draw itself under position.

widget.prompt: Take s(t) = t³. Drag to the one instant where the particle is momentarily at REST — where the velocity curve underneath touches zero.
widget.successFeedback: t = 0, where v = 3t² = 0. The particle stops for an instant — and then carries straight on in the SAME direction, because v never goes negative. Momentarily at rest is not the same as turning round: for that, v must change SIGN. It is the saddle from curve analysis, wearing a physics hat.
widget.lowFeedback: Velocity is still positive here — the particle is still moving. Keep sliding right.
widget.highFeedback: Past the stopping instant — velocity is positive again. Come back left.

predict.prompt: You'll ride the tangent to x = 0. When you arrive, the tangent line will be tilting…
predict.reveal: At x = 0 the tangent lies flat — slope exactly 0. Flat tangents are where a curve CAN turn: the derivative's zeros mark the candidate hilltops and valley floors — though not every zero is a turn, and this very curve, s = t³, flattens at 0 and then keeps on climbing.

cml.actionGoal: Move along a function and coordinate position, local slope, and derivative graph.

explanationVariants: v = 3(t − 1)(t − 3) is zero at t = 1 and t = 3, and it CHANGES SIGN at both — so the particle actually reverses at each.
Zero velocity means momentarily at rest. Reversing needs a sign change, which is a stronger claim.

widget.prompt: s(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t, so v(t) = 3(t − 1)(t − 3). At how many instants is the particle at rest?

commonErrors.feedback: 3(t − 1)(t − 3) = 0 has TWO roots: t = 1 and t = 3. The particle stops at both.
The velocity certainly reaches zero — at t = 1 and t = 3.
A quadratic velocity has at most two zeros, and here it has exactly two.

widget.fallbackFeedback: v = 3(t − 1)(t − 3) = 0 at t = 1 and t = 3: two instants of rest.

steps.body:
Reading the motion is reading two signs:

**v > 0** — moving forward (right, up, positive direction).
**v < 0** — moving backward.
**a > 0** — the velocity is increasing.
**a < 0** — the velocity is decreasing.

Note that a > 0 does **not** mean 'speeding up'. A car reversing with positive acceleration is slowing down.

explanationVariants: v(2) = 12 − 24 + 9 = −3 (moving backward) and a(2) = 12 − 12 = 0 (velocity momentarily unchanging).
Zero acceleration does not mean stopped — the particle is travelling backward at 3 units per second and, for an instant, steadily.

widget.prompt: At t = 2: v = −3 and a = 0. What is the particle doing?

options.label: Moving backward at a steady speed, for that instant.
options.feedback: Right. Negative velocity means backward; zero acceleration means the velocity is momentarily not changing at all.

options.label: Stopped.
options.feedback: Stopped means v = 0. Here v = −3 — it is moving, just in the negative direction.

options.label: Slowing down.
options.feedback: Slowing down needs the SPEED to be falling, which needs v and a to have opposite signs. Here a = 0, so the speed is momentarily constant.

options.label: Speeding up.
options.feedback: With a = 0 the velocity is not changing at that instant, so the speed is not increasing either.

steps.body: Where is it, when it stops?
hints: First find WHEN it is at rest: solve v = 3(t − 1)(t − 3) = 0.
That gives t = 1 and t = 3. The question asks for the position at the FIRST of these.
explanationVariants: v = 0 first at t = 1, and s(1) = 1 − 6 + 9 = 4.
Velocity told you WHEN; only the position function can tell you WHERE.

widget.prompt: s(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t. Where is the particle the FIRST time it comes to rest?

commonErrors.feedback: That is WHEN it stops (t = 1). The question asks WHERE: s(1) = 1 − 6 + 9 = 4.
That is s(3), the position at the SECOND stop. The first stop is at t = 1, where s = 4.
That is the second time it stops. The first is t = 1, and its position there is 4.

widget.fallbackFeedback: v = 0 first at t = 1, and s(1) = 4.

takeaways: s says where, v = s′ says how fast and which way, a = s″ says whether that is changing.
v = 0 means momentarily at rest. Turning round is a stronger claim — it needs v to change SIGN.
a > 0 does NOT mean speeding up. That comparison is the next lesson.
steps.teaser: Next: the sign rule that finally settles speeding up versus slowing down.

concept.body: Differentiate once for velocity, twice for acceleration — and substitute only at the very end. The position tells you WHERE; only the velocity can tell you how fast; only the acceleration can tell you whether that is changing.

explanationVariants: s = t³ gives v = 3t² and a = 6t, so a(2) = 12.

widget.prompt: s(t) = t³. Find the acceleration at t = 2.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the coefficient of t in a = 6t. Substitute t = 2: a = 12.
